questions.title: Activity Selection
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Timeline showing compatible activities
questions.problem_statement:
You are given N activities. Each activity has a start time and a finish time. Select the maximum number of activities that one person can complete, assuming a person can attend only one activity at a time. An activity can be selected if its start time is greater than or equal to the finish time of the previously selected activity. Sort activities by finish time before selecting them.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-01 — Activity Selection](/diagrams/m20/m20_01.png)

Explanation: Choose (1,3), then (4,6), then (6,8). Each selected activity starts when or after the previous one finishes.
questions.input_format: First line: integer N. Next N lines: two integers S and F, the start and finish times of one activity.
questions.output_format: Print the maximum number of non-overlapping activities.
hints: Time complexity target is O(N log N).

questions.output_format: Print each merged interval on its own line as L R.

questions.title: Minimum Number of Platforms
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Arrival/departure event timeline
questions.problem_statement:
A railway station has N trains. Each train has an arrival time and a departure time written as an integer in 24-hour HHMM format (for example, 900 means 09:00 and 1430 means 14:30). Find the minimum number of platforms needed so that every train can arrive and depart without waiting for a platform. If a train arrives at exactly the time another train departs, the arriving train needs a separate platform at that moment; the departing train still occupies its platform at its departure time.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-03 — Minimum Number of Platforms](/diagrams/m20/m20_03.png)

Explanation: The first train leaves at 9:10. The trains arriving at 9:40 and 9:50 overlap until the second train leaves at 12:00, so the maximum simultaneous trains is 2.
questions.input_format: First line: integer N. Second line: N arrival times. Third line: N departure times.
questions.output_format: Print the minimum number of platforms required.
questions.constraints: 1 ≤ N ≤ 100000; 0 ≤ time ≤ 2359; the last two digits of every time must be ≤ 59; each arrival is earlier than its departure on the same day
hints: Time complexity target is O(N log N).

extra_fields.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
extra_fields.input_format: First line: integer N. Second line: N arrival times. Third line: N departure times.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the minimum number of platforms required.

questions.title: Fractional Knapsack
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Value-to-weight ratio table
questions.problem_statement:
A bag can carry at most W units of weight. Each of N items has a positive weight and value. You may take an entire item or any fraction of it, and the value of a fraction is proportional to the fraction taken. Choose portions of items to maximize the total value without exceeding W. Print the result rounded to exactly two decimal places using round-half-up: if the third decimal digit is 5 or greater, increase the second decimal digit by one (carrying to the integer part if needed). In Java, use Locale.US when formatting so the decimal separator is a dot.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-04 — Fractional Knapsack](/diagrams/m20/m20_04.png)

Explanation: Take the first item (value 60), the second item (value 100), and 20 of the third item’s 30 weight, worth 80. The total value is 240.00. For Java formatting, use Locale.US to ensure a dot decimal separator.
questions.input_format: First line: N W. Next N lines: weight and value of each item.
questions.output_format: Print the maximum value rounded half-up to exactly two digits after the decimal point, using a dot as the decimal separator (for example, 240.00).
hints: Time complexity target is O(N log N).

extra_fields.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
extra_fields.input_format: First line: N W. Next N lines: weight and value of each item.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the maximum value rounded half-up to exactly two digits after the decimal point, using a dot as the decimal separator (for example, 240.00).

questions.title: Job Sequencing with Deadlines
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Deadline slots with chosen jobs
questions.problem_statement:
Each job takes exactly one unit of time and has a deadline and a positive profit. Only one job can be performed in each time slot, and a job earns its profit only if it is completed on or before its deadline. Schedule a subset of jobs to maximize total profit. Report the number of jobs in a maximum-profit schedule and that schedule’s total profit.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-05 — Job Sequencing with Deadlines](/diagrams/m20/m20_05.png)

Explanation: Schedule the job with profit 100 in slot 2 and the job with profit 27 in slot 1. Both jobs finish on or before their deadlines, so the number of jobs is 2 and the total profit is 127.
questions.input_format: First line: N. Next N lines: deadline and profit for each job.
questions.output_format: Print two integers: the number of jobs in a maximum-profit schedule, followed by its total profit.

extra_fields.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming

questions.title: Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Intervals and arrow positions
questions.problem_statement:
Each balloon is represented by a horizontal interval [L, R]. An arrow shot vertically at coordinate X bursts every balloon whose interval contains X. Find the minimum number of arrows needed to burst all balloons. Since endpoints can be as large as 10^9 in magnitude, avoid subtracting coordinates in a sorting comparator; in Java, use Integer.compare(a[1], b[1]) to compare end coordinates safely.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-06 — Minimum Arrows to Burst Balloons](/diagrams/m20/m20_06.png)

Explanation: Place one arrow at coordinate 6 to burst [1,6] and [2,8]. Place another at 12 to burst [7,12] and [10,16].
questions.input_format: First line: N. Next N lines: L R for each balloon.
questions.output_format: Print the minimum number of arrows.
hints: Time complexity target is O(N log N).

extra_fields.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
extra_fields.input_format: First line: N. Next N lines: L R for each balloon.
extra_fields.output_format: Print the minimum number of arrows.

questions.title: Coin Change with Fewest Coins (Canonical Coins)
questions.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming
questions.objective: Greedy Algorithms: Coin stack breakdown
questions.problem_statement:
You are given a target amount A and an unlimited supply of coins with denominations 1, 5, 10, and 25. Find the minimum number of coins needed to make exactly A. For this coin system, repeatedly taking the largest coin that does not exceed the remaining amount gives an optimal answer. Since a coin of value 1 is always available, every non-negative amount can be formed and the answer is never -1. To process large amounts efficiently, use integer division (A / coin) to count how many coins of a denomination can be taken, rather than subtracting the coin repeatedly.

Write all classes in Main.java. Only class Main may be declared public; declare any other classes without the public keyword.

![M20-08 — Coin Change with Fewest Coins (Canonical Coins)](/diagrams/m20/m20_08.png)

Explanation: Take 25 + 25 + 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 63, using six coins.
questions.input_format: One integer A.
questions.output_format: Print the minimum number of coins.

extra_fields.module: Module 20: Greedy Algorithms and Dynamic Programming

extra_fields.output_format: Print the minimum number of coins.
